pinterest.title: Diamond Buying Guide: Which of the 4Cs Matters Most, and How to Check a Grading Report
pinterest.description: A diamond buying guide that ranks the 4Cs by what actually changes how a stone looks on the hand. For a round brilliant, settle the cut grade first, then balance colour, clarity and carat. Carat measures weight, not size. Before paying, type the GIA or IGI report number into the lab's own website and match it to the girdle inscription. Plus lab-grown vs natural, fluorescence and a shortlist checklist.

pinterest.title: Diamond Certificate Check: How to Verify a GIA or IGI Report Before You Pay
pinterest.description: A grading report is the independent record of a diamond's characteristics, but only if it belongs to the stone in front of you. Type the report number into the lab's own website yourself, rather than following a link or QR code someone hands you. Match the online record to the paper report and the number laser inscribed on the girdle. And remember a grading report is not a valuation.

pinterest.title: Lab Grown vs Natural Diamond: What Is Really Different, and What to Get in Writing
pinterest.description: A laboratory-grown diamond is a real diamond, not an imitation, with essentially the same optical, physical and chemical properties as a mined one. The difference is origin. Both GIA and IGI report on lab-grown stones and mark origin with a girdle inscription. Get natural or lab-grown confirmed in writing on both the receipt and the report. Neither is automatically the more ethical choice.

slides: Most diamond advice is written by someone with a tray of stones to sell you. Here is what actually changes how a diamond looks on the hand.
Cut first. For a round brilliant, cut has the greatest effect on sparkle: brightness, fire and scintillation. Then balance colour, clarity and carat.
Carat is weight, not size. Two stones of the same weight can face up quite differently once set.
Clarity in proportion. Many inclusions can't be seen without magnification. 'Eye-clean' is a trade term, not a GIA grade, so view the stone face up yourself.
Check the report before any money moves. Type the GIA or IGI number into the lab's own website, then match it to the girdle inscription.
Lab-grown or natural? Both are real diamonds. Get the origin confirmed in writing on the receipt and the report.
Kimberley Process compliant speaks to one problem: rough diamonds funding rebel conflict. Ask your jeweller what else they know about origin.

instagram_carousel.caption:
Most advice on choosing a diamond comes from someone with stones to sell. Our new diamond buying guide ranks the 4Cs by what actually changes how a stone looks on the hand.

A few things worth knowing before your first appointment:
For a round brilliant, settle the cut grade first. Only round brilliants get a GIA cut grade, so judge fancy shapes like ovals and pears face up, in person.
Judge colour against the metal you plan to use, in daylight as well as shop lighting.
GIA calls 1.00, 1.50 and 2.00 carats "magic sizes", yet a 0.99 carat stone is very hard to tell apart by eye. Ask to see stones just under each one.
Fluorescence rarely changes how a stone looks. View a fluorescent stone in daylight beside others of the same grade.
Before paying, type the report number into the lab's own website and match it to the girdle inscription.
Carrying the ring abroad? Keep it in your hand luggage, tell your insurer your travel dates, and pack copies of the report and receipt separately.

The full guide, with a shortlist checklist, is linked in bio.

Which C are you weighing up most? Tell us below, or chat with a Wedded Advisor if the proposal or wedding is heading overseas.
